vignette:
He is 40, a married Middle Eastern man who works as a software engineer, and when he talks about the earthquake, he does so in a careful, almost methodical way at first, as if he is debugging a system and trying to reconstruct the exact sequence of failures. He had been visiting family in his home country with his wife and young daughter when it happened. It was just before dawn. He remembers waking to a low groan in the walls, then the violent shaking that seemed to come from everywhere at once. At first he thought he was still dreaming. Then he heard glass breaking, his mother shouting from the next room, and his daughter screaming his name.

He says the worst part is not the shaking itself but the few seconds in which he could not reach her. A wardrobe had tipped into the hallway, blocking the bedroom door. He threw his shoulder against it over and over while the floor moved under him. Dust filled the air so completely that he could not see more than a few feet in front of him. He remembers thinking, with absolute clarity, that his family was going to die and that he was failing them in the final moments. When he finally got the door open, his daughter was crouched under part of the bed, crying, and his wife was trying to pull debris away from her with bleeding hands.

They made it outside with his parents and several neighbors, but the street looked unfamiliar, as if a familiar map had been rewritten in seconds. Buildings had split open. Car alarms blared. People were running in different directions, shouting names. There were aftershocks all morning. He spent hours helping lift concrete and carrying water, switching between frantic action and moments in which everything went muffled and far away. Later they learned that two members of his extended family had been killed. He does not describe himself as someone who cries easily, but when he says this, his eyes fix on the floor and his voice flattens.

When he returns home weeks later, he expects that being back in his own apartment, back at his desk, back in routines and code reviews and school pickups, will make the feeling pass. Instead, he notices how quickly his body reacts to small things. If a truck rattles past the building, his chest seizes before he can think. If his phone vibrates suddenly on the table, he startles so hard that coworkers look up. He begins checking exits everywhere he goes: restaurants, the masjid, his daughter’s classroom during parent events. In meetings he prefers to sit near the door. He tells himself this is just practical.

Sleep becomes the place where the earthquake keeps happening. He wakes drenched in sweat, already on his feet, sometimes grabbing his wife’s arm hard enough that she tells him later he frightened her. On some nights he paces the apartment to make sure nothing can fall, straightening shelves, moving heavy objects lower, testing windows. His wife asks him to come back to bed, but he cannot settle. He says that once he lies down, he starts listening for vibrations in the walls.

At work, where he used to be known as calm and precise, he finds himself making mistakes that bother him more than they should. He reads the same block of code three times and still cannot hold it in mind. When a production issue comes up and messages begin stacking in Slack, his heart races with the same helpless urgency he felt in the hallway that morning. He becomes irritable with junior engineers, then ashamed afterward. He starts staying late, not because he is getting more done, but because tasks that used to take an hour now stretch across an afternoon.

His world narrows in quiet ways. He avoids news about earthquakes and floods, but he also avoids calls from relatives overseas because he dreads hearing another story of loss. He no longer wants to visit high-rise offices downtown. He has stopped taking his daughter to the science museum because one exhibit hall has suspended lights and exposed beams that make him uneasy. His wife notices that he rarely laughs now. He is physically present with his family, but often somewhere else inside himself, as though part of him is still standing in that dust-filled hallway.

He feels guilty that he survived when others did not, guilty that he brought his wife and daughter there, guilty that he could not protect everyone. He knows, rationally, that he did what he could. He says this the way he would explain a fact to someone else. But emotionally he remains unconvinced. Months later, he still scans ceilings, still calculates how fast he could get his family out of a room, still feels his body brace against a danger no one else can see. Even in safety, he lives as if the ground might give way again.
